label: Search Exceeded the Scope of a Search Incident to Arrest
motion_heading: The Search Exceeded the Limited Scope of a Search Incident to Arrest

review_conditions.display_note: You aren't sure yet whether the search went beyond what a search incident to arrest allows. This section was drafted anyway; establish where your client was, whether they were secured, and exactly what was searched before filing, or cut this section.

Even when the arrestee is secured, a vehicle search incident to arrest is allowed if it was reasonable to believe evidence of the offense of arrest was in the vehicle. Expect the prosecution to argue this, especially for drug or DUI arrests (open containers); be ready to explain why no such evidence could be expected.

Police had some basis to think the container held pocket or purse items, so expect the prosecution to argue it was “immediately associated with the person” (Crawford; Pitka) and could be searched without exigency. Address what the officer actually knew at the time of the search.

sentences.text: A search incident to a lawful arrest may extend only to the arrestee's person and the area within the arrestee's immediate control — the area from which the arrestee might gain possession of a weapon or destructible evidence.
That justification does not extend to searching rooms other than the one in which the arrest occurs, or closed or concealed areas in that room.
“[S]pecial rules govern when closed containers can be searched incident to a lawful arrest and without a warrant.”
Unless there is an exigent circumstance such as a danger that the arrestee will seize a weapon or destroy evidence, an officer must seize items and obtain a search warrant to inspect them.
However, there is an exception to the exigency requirement when an item is “immediately associated with the person.”
These items are exempt because they are “often worn on the person and generally serve the same function as clothing pockets,” which may lawfully be searched incident to arrest.

In *Crawford*, the Alaska Supreme Court held that the center console of a car is “immediately associated with the driver’s person” because it is permanently located next to the driver and is commonly used to hold items often held in pockets, such as “money, a cellular telephone, and personal hygiene items.”

The Court of Appeals subsequently explained that not all containers “capable of holding personal items” may be searched; instead, “the police must have some articulable basis for believing that the container is *generally* used, or is actually being used *in that particular instance*, to store items that would normally be kept in a pocket or a purse.”
Based on that rule, the Court of Appeals held that a built-in ashtray was not “immediately associated with the person” based on the information known to the officer at the time of the search.

There is no evidence that this type of container is generally used to store items that would normally be kept in a pocket or purse, and no evidence that {client} was using it to store personal effects such as money or a phone.

Police may search a vehicle incident to a recent occupant's arrest only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of the passenger compartment at the time of the search, or it is reasonable to believe the vehicle contains evidence of the offense of arrest.
Police generally must obtain a warrant before searching the data on a cell phone seized incident to arrest.
A search that is remote in time or place from the arrest is not incident to the arrest.

practice_notes: A search incident to arrest requires a lawful arrest — if the arrest itself lacked probable cause, argue that too; this issue assumes the arrest was lawful.
_author_notes: REVIEW CAREFULLY (legal judgment not yet reviewed): this issue is suggested when q_sita_searched includes another room or closed area, phone data, a closed container, something searched later or elsewhere, or 'not sure'; or a vehicle while your client was secured or taken away (Gant). The person and the area within reach never suggest it on their own, and neither does a vehicle searched while your client stood nearby unrestrained.
